Covered schema enforcement, validation/guardrails, streaming responses with function/tool calls, and security considerations for a regulated analytics customer. transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood Product), Tom Lewis (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Brightline CTO), Maya Lopez (Brightline ML Eng), Samir Khan (Brightline SecOps), Ellen Wu (Brightline PM)

Auto-summary: Demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool-calling. Walked through Console, API snippets, and Redwood Optimize tips for schema validation, guardrails, and streaming behavior. Security questions about KMS, audit logs, and VPC were raised.

[00:00] Sophie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining  we'll give a 45ish minute walkthrough of structured output and the tool calling stuff, and leave time for Q&A. I'm Sophie, AE at Redwood. Carlos will run through the technical demo.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: Hi all, yeah I'll share my screen in a sec  quick agenda: API + Console demo of JSON mode, function-calling example (we call it tool-calling here), schema enforcement, and some guardrail patterns.
[00:34] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Our main goals are deterministic outputs for downstream pipelines and safe tool invocations  we have a stricter validation step in our ETL so we want the model to always return valid JSON or error codes.
[00:48] Maya Lopez: And latency/cost tradeoffs  we process real-time analytics, so 100ms-ish is ideal, but we'll accept slightly higher if it reduces post-processing.
[01:05] Carlos Mendez: Totally, we'll talk about batching/quantization tradeoffs later. For now demo  switching to Console... apologies if auto-caption is a little off, sometimes it says 'Red good' instead of Redwood.
[01:22] [screen share noise] Tom Lewis: Opening the Structured Output tab  here we have JSON mode where you can paste a JSON schema, and then the runtime will validate responses against that schema and optionally block or coerce outputs.
[01:40] Maya Lopez: Quick question, does validate run at token level or after full response?
[01:48] Carlos Mendez: Good question. Validation is post-response by default, but we support streaming validation hooks. For example, partial output can be validated as chunks arrive and we can trigger a function call mid-stream if certain fields are ready  we demo that shortly.
[02:10] Samir Khan: On the security front: where does the schema live? Is it customer-managed? We need to prove it can't leak into logs.
[02:21] Sophie Chen: Schema definitions are stored in the customer's project space; for Dedicated/Private customers you can opt to keep schema artifacts in your VPC or on-prem storage. Logs can be redacted and we have KMS integrations for encryption.
[02:38] [00:02 clip of typing] Carlos Mendez: Alright I'm going to run a function-calling example  we're going to ask the model to return an order JSON for a purchase event and then invoke an internal 'save_order' tool.
[02:58] [02:58] Carlos Mendez (demo): Posting request to the API with "function": "save_order", schema attached. Note: in Console we have a toggle for 'enforce_schema' (hard) vs 'warn_only'. I'll set enforce for this run.
[03:20] [03:20] Model (simulated): {
  "order_id": "ord-7923",
  "customer": { "id": "cust-112", "name": "Alice M." },
  "items": [ { "sku": "SKU-100", "qty": 2 } ],
  "total": 49.98
}
[03:45] Carlos Mendez: The runtime validated the JSON and then we triggered the save_order tool via function call; in Console you'll see the tool invocation and the tool response. If validation failed, we can either reject, return an error object, or try to repair via a Rewrite policy.
[04:05] Raj Patel: Can we see a failure mode where model returns malformed JSON?
[04:12] Carlos Mendez: Yes  switching to warn_only and forcing an edge case  sending a prompt that often produces trailing commas.
[04:28] [04:28] Model (simulated): {
  "order_id": "ord-7924",
  "customer": "Bob",
}
[04:45] Carlos Mendez: That comes back as invalid; in warn_only Console flags it and returns the raw output plus validation errors. In enforce_schema mode we block the response and return structured error payload: { code: "schema_violation", details: [ ... ] } and optionally call an error handler tool.
[05:02] Maya Lopez: Is there an auto-repair? We want the model to sometimes fix minor formatting issues instead of blocking.
[05:11] Carlos Mendez: Yes, we have a 'repair' policy: the runtime can re-prompt a model to correct output or run a deterministic repair function. Repair costs an extra token/action so there's a tradeoff. We showed a 'smart_repair' option in Redwood Optimize that suggests when repair is worth it based on downstream cost.
[05:35] [05:35] Priya Kapoor: Just to add, from product side the Optimize recommendations can flag schemas that are too permissive leading to more repair calls. It surfaces token-cost estimates per policy.
[05:50] [06:00] [short silence / typing] Tom Lewis (Redwood): Next up is streaming + partial tool calls  example: the model streams event fields as they are generated and when the 'customer' object is complete we call 'lookup_customer_profile' tool to enrich data mid-stream.
[06:23] [06:23] Model stream chunk: { "order_id": "ord-8001" }
[06:30] [06:30] Model stream chunk: { "customer": { "id": "cust-443" } }
[06:42] Tom Lewis: At this point we call the customer-profile tool  the tool returns profile data and the runtime merges it into the output before completing. This reduces downstream joins and keeps latency bounded.
[07:00] Raj Patel: How do you ensure tool side effects are idempotent if stream retries happen?
[07:08] Carlos Mendez: We recommend idempotent design for tools, use request ids and Redwood supports at-least-once vs exactly-once semantics per tool. You can also tag tool calls with a unique invocation token so downstream services can dedupe.
[07:25] Samir Khan: What about permissions? We don't want tools to leak PII or call network services outside allowed scopes.
[07:33] Sophie Chen: Tools run in a restricted runtime. Access policies are managed via RBAC and can be restricted by project and role; audit logs capture tool inputs/outputs. For Private deployments you can completely isolate tool execution into your VPC.
[07:52] [08:00] Maya Lopez: Can we see the API snippet? I want to know how to attach a JSON schema and how the function signature looks.
[08:08] Carlos Mendez: Sure  pasting the curl:

curl https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{
  "model":"redwood-xt-1",
  "mode":"json",
  "schema": <JSON_SCHEMA>,
  "functions": [{"name":"save_order","args_schema": <TOOL_SCHEMA> }],
  "prompt": "Create order for user Alice..."
}'

[08:46] Carlos Mendez: In SDKs it's a typed call: client.generate({ mode: 'json', schema, functions, enforce_schema: true })  the response contains a status and either a 'result' (validated) or 'error' payload.
[09:05] Raj Patel: Do you support complex schema types  nested arrays, union types, optional fields?
[09:12] Carlos Mendez: Yep  we support JSON Schema Draft-07 features commonly used: nested objects, arrays, oneOf/anyOf patterns, and custom validation hooks. A note: extremely permissive oneOf logic can make validation slower so Optimize will flag expensive schemas.
[09:35] [09:35] Ellen Wu: How do we test schemas at scale? We have thousands of event types and don't want to hand-run tests.
[09:44] Tom Lewis: In Console we have a Schema Test harness  upload examples, run batch validation against the model and measure pass rates. The POC sandbox we provision will include an automated run and a CSV of failures.
[10:02] Maya Lopez: Any tips for schema design to minimize repair calls?
[10:09] Priya Kapoor: Keep required fields explicit, avoid overly broad unions, and prefer enumerations where possible. Also set 'coerce_types' flag only when you want downstream leniency. Optimize suggests a schema revision with expected token impact.
[10:30] [10:40] Carlos Mendez: Now a short deep dive: guardrails. There are three levels  pre-prompt constraints, runtime schema validation, and post-hoc detectors. We also integrate model evaluation sets to detect regressions when you roll new model variants.
[10:58] [11:10] Maya Lopez: Show us an example of blocking an unsafe tool call?
[11:16] Carlos Mendez: Triggering a policy that denies network tool calls if input contains PII tags; runtime will return a structured deny object and log the attempt.
[11:32] [11:32] Model simulated response: { "error": "tool_denied", "reason": "PII_policy_violation" }
[11:45] Samir Khan: On logging  can audit logs be sent to our SIEM? We have strict retention rules.
[11:52] Sophie Chen: Yes  logs can be forwarded via secure connectors to SIEMs, and retention is configurable for Dedicated/Private customers. For Hosted we keep standard retention but can offer extended retention as an add-on.
[12:10] [12:20] Raj Patel: If we pick Dedicated vs Hosted, what changes for structured output? Any different capabilities?
[12:28] Priya Kapoor: Core runtime features are the same; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity, custom kernels, and the option to store schema/artifacts in your VPC. Private gives you even more control including offline on-prem installs.
[12:45] Raj Patel: Good. Cost question  is enforcing schema more expensive?
[12:52] Carlos Mendez: There is a small overhead for validation (CPU/latency), and repair flows add tokens. Optimize will show estimated cost per 10k requests for different enforcement policies.
[13:08] [13:08] Maya Lopez: Can we see a live run where the model needs to call two tools mid-flow? One to enrich profile, another to check fraud scoring.
[13:20] Carlos Mendez: Yes  running that now. First chunk emits order and customer id, we call lookup_profile, then after items are present we call fraud_check tool.
[13:38] [13:38] Model stream: { "order_id":"ord-9003" }
[13:45] [13:45] Tool call -> lookup_profile invoked with { "customer_id": "cust-900" }
[13:52] [13:52] Tool response -> profile returned: { "loyalty_level": "gold" }
[14:00] [14:00] Tool call -> fraud_check invoked with { "order": { ... } }
[14:08] [14:08] Tool response -> fraud_check: { "score": 0.02, "action": "accept" }
[14:16] Carlos Mendez: Runtime merged the profile + fraud result and completed output. In the Console trace you can expand each tool call and see inputs/outputs and timestamps.
[14:30] Raj Patel: How long are traces retained? We have retention policy requirements.
[14:36] Sophie Chen: Traces and audit logs retention configurable; default hosted retention is 30 days, Dedicated can be extended, Private you're in control. Traces can be exported off-platform.
[14:50] Samir Khan: Does the platform redact PII automatically?
[14:56] Tom Lewis: We offer automatic PII detection and optional redaction. It's configurable per project and you can choose token-level masking for logs.
[15:08] [15:10] Maya Lopez: If we need deterministic ordering of arrays in schema, does runtime guarantee preservation?
[15:18] Carlos Mendez: JSON arrays order is preserved by default; if you need strong determinism we recommend post-validate canonicalization step that can be part of the tool chain.
[15:35] [15:40] Ellen Wu: For our data pipeline, we want an error object with standardized codes to trigger retries  is that supported?
[15:48] Priya Kapoor: Yes, error payloads have machine-readable 'code' and 'retryable' flag. You can map those to pipeline handlers.
[16:00] [16:10] Raj Patel: Can we limit model variants? We may only want a specific, quantized variant in production.
[16:18] Sophie Chen: Absolutely. You can pin a model version in deployment configs and set fallback options. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles for that model to hit latency targets.
[16:35] [16:40] Maya Lopez: About quantization  are there known regressions for structured output? Some quantized models hallucinate more.
[16:48] Carlos Mendez: Yep, that's why we tie quality monitoring to eval sets. Optimize runs regression checks when you switch quantization profiles or model variants and flags schema pass-rate drops.
[17:05] [17:10] Samir Khan: On PCI / PHI concerns, do you offer on-prem isolated options for high-sensitivity workloads?
[17:18] Sophie Chen: Yes, Private deployment is designed for that. It includes audit, key management via customer KMS/HSM, and the option for air-gapped installs.
[17:34] [17:40] Ellen Wu: Let's talk about ramp plan  if we start with a small pilot, what's the typical timeline for Dedicated?
[17:48] Priya Kapoor: Pilot can start within days with a sandbox. Dedicated provisioning depends on capacity and contract but often 2-4 weeks. Private/on-prem longer due to infra.
[18:05] [18:10] Carlos Mendez: Quick demo wrap  I'm going to show the Schema Test harness results. Here's a sample run: 200 examples, 182 passed, 18 failed. The Console shows failure buckets and sample diffs.
[18:30] [18:30] Model: diff -> Expected 'customer.id' string but got number in 10 examples.
[18:38] Maya Lopez: That mismatch is exactly the reason we want strong enforcement.
[18:43] Carlos Mendez: For those cases you can set 'auto_coerce_numbers' true to coerce integers to strings, or enforce and send back errors for manual remediation. Optimize will recommend the cheaper option based on downstream cost.
[18:55] [19:00] Raj Patel: Any example infra we should run for us? We have a Spark-based upstream and need connectors.
[19:08] Tom Lewis: We provide an event sink connector that writes validated JSON into S3 or Kafka. For realtime low-latency you can stream to Kafka; we also have a direct API integration for microservices.
[19:22] Maya Lopez: How are token costs reported when using tool calls? Do tools consume tokens?
[19:29] Carlos Mendez: Tool calls themselves don't consume model tokens but they add runtime overhead; however if the repair flow re-queries the model that's billed. We show per-request breakdown in Console with token counts and tool costs.
[19:45] [20:00] Samir Khan: We need to run a security review  can you share the compliance pack and a contact for privacy/security?
[20:09] Sophie Chen: I'll send the SOC 2, ISO, and a direct SecOps contact. Also will include KMS/HSM docs and the architecture for private deployments.
[20:22] [20:22] Ellen Wu: Would be great to have a sample contract SLA for Dedicated as well.
[20:28] Sophie Chen: Yep, attaching sample SLA in follow-up.
[20:35] [20:40] Carlos Mendez: I'm going to simulate a POC run now using their example schema that Maya provided earlier  note: in this demo I reduced the dataset to 50 examples.
[20:58] [21:00] Model run started  showing batch validation UI  50 examples -> 46 pass, 4 fail. Failure reasons: type mismatch, missing required field.
[21:16] Maya Lopez: Ok good. Can we get the raw logs from that run?
[21:22] Carlos Mendez: Yes the sandbox export will include raw model outputs and validation diffs; we'll upload to the POC folder in the project.
[21:35] [21:40] Raj Patel: For the POC, we want to measure end-to-end time including enrichment tool calls. Can you instrument that?
[21:48] Tom Lewis: Yes we'll include per-step latency traces and a heatmap of time spent in model vs tools vs network.
[21:58] [22:00] Priya Kapoor: A note about maintainability  schemas should be versioned. Redwood supports schema versioning and rollout policies so you can canary a new schema and fallback.
[22:16] Maya Lopez: How do rollouts handle incompatible schema changes?
[22:22] Carlos Mendez: You can set a compatibility policy  if the new schema fails the canary threshold, we automatically rollback requests to the previous schema or route to a fallback model.
[22:35] [22:40] Raj Patel: That is helpful. Any limitations we should know about?
[22:45] Carlos Mendez: A few: extremely large schemas (>1MB) can slow validation; very high-frequency streaming with many mid-stream tool calls increases complexity and can impact cost. We advise performance testing in the sandbox.
[23:00] [23:10] Samir Khan: On legal/procurement  what's the usual contract length and entry price for Dedicated?
[23:18] Sophie Chen: Typical is 12 36 month commitments; entry pricing varies based on capacity. I'll include a sample quote with the follow-up.
[23:30] [23:40] Ellen Wu: Any references of similar customers in analytics/health?
[23:47] Sophie Chen: We have a case study with a financial analytics customer who used schema enforcement and tool-calling to reduce post-processing by 60%  I'll share that link.
[23:58] [24:00] Maya Lopez: Quick nit  the Console UI sometimes mislabels function-calls as 'tools' and the transcript might be confusing.
[24:06] Tom Lewis: Yep that's a UX note we have on the roadmap  unify naming.
[24:14] [24:20] Carlos Mendez: We're approaching Q&A  anyone have outstanding technical questions?
[24:28] Raj Patel: I'm curious about multi-region redundancy for tool endpoints  we have EU data residency needs.
[24:36] Sophie Chen: You can pin region routing policies and have tool endpoints in-region; for strict residency pick Dedicated or Private in the target region.
[24:50] [25:00] Maya Lopez: Anything else on monitoring?
[25:07] Priya Kapoor: Console has per-route dashboards showing schema pass rate, tool invocation rates, token breakdown, and latencies. Alerts can be tied to uptime or quality regressions.
[25:22] [25:30] Samir Khan: For data retention terms, we'll need custom agreements.
[25:36] Sophie Chen: Understood  that'll be part of contract discussions.
[25:42] [26:00] Carlos Mendez: Final quick demo: show the function-call audit trace export. You can download a CSV of tool calls with timestamps, inputs, outputs (optionally redacted).
[26:18] [26:18] Model sample entry: { "time":"2026-03-02T16:13:45Z", "tool":"save_order", "status":"success" }
[26:30] Maya Lopez: This looks good. We're interested in trying the sandbox.
[26:35] Sophie Chen: Great  we'll provision the trial by 2026-03-05. Carlos will run the first schema tests and share results.
[26:50] [27:00] Q&A section with smaller clarifications and a few mis-transcribed words  minute markers omitted here for brevity.
[27:20] [approx later] Sophie Chen (recap): Quick recap  we'll send recording and slides, SOC2 docs, sample SLA, provision sandbox and run Maya's schema against 200 examples. Next call POC scoping on 2026-03-09.
[27:42] Raj Patel: Thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.
[27:50] Maya Lopez: Thanks everyone.
[28:00] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription: occasional caption errors (e.g., "Red good" for Redwood, "V P C" for VPC), speaker overlaps and short crosstalk. The transcript has been lightly cleaned but retains speech artifacts.
